**1.** A radio report announces that by 2050, farming in Massachusetts will resemble farming in Georgia. Will we one day harvest syrup from the boreal forest and peaches from Massachusetts?

Yet, I am reminded of the documentary on gleaning, in which a compassionate priest observes that those who glean out of spiritual hunger deserve to be nourished as well. 

**5.** Whether an ecosystem of the yard, the field, or the mind: growing these cucumbers feels more like art than science, more akin to a daydream than global action—assuming we can even separate the two. Yet, as I dig into the soil, I sense a profound alterity—a vital, magnificent, non-human freedom. Here, I tend a plot of land that ultimately grounds me in return.

We are living through a profound rewrite of the natural world. As climate change unpredictably alters global agricultural regions, the historical boundaries of what can grow—and where—are shifting beneath our feet. Crops that have sustained civilizations for millennia and native trees that have defined regional landscapes for centuries are increasingly forced out of their natural ranges, uncertain of their ability to thrive in an unpredictable future. 

This ecological disorientation takes place against a harrowing backdrop of human suffering and environmental decay. The daily rhythm of modern life is constantly punctuated by news of war, pervasive pollution, and devastating droughts. It can often feel as though the world is consuming itself, leaving individuals burdened by a quiet, persistent existential dread.

In the face of such overwhelming global crises, turning to a modest backyard patch or windowsill planter might seem almost trivial. It is true, of course, that small-scale gardening cannot single-handedly solve global famine or reverse the geopolitical structures that cause it. Yet, its true value lies elsewhere. The act of growing food and flowers satisfies a profound spiritual hunger—a deep-seated human need for tangible connection in a world that increasingly feels fragmented and disembodied.

Ultimately, cultivating the land is far more than a practical chore; it acts as a quiet form of artistic daydreaming. When we place a seed in the earth, we engage in a creative partnership with time, light, and soil. This intimate practice pulls us out of our human-centric anxieties and grounds us in a broader, non-human vital force. In the garden, surrounded by the slow, indifferent resilience of growth and decay, we find a tether back to life itself.
outputs.L4:
It arrives in a relentless, digital deluge: headlines of wildfires consuming ancient forests, the terrifying metrics of rising sea levels, and the heartbreaking fallout of geopolitical violence broadcast in real time. To live in the modern world is to exist in a state of quiet, chronic despair. Faced with disasters of such apocalyptic scale, the human spirit recoils into a profound sense of helplessness. Recycling a plastic container or turning off a light switch suddenly feels less like a meaningful contribution and more like a cruel joke—a water pistol brought to a raging inferno. 

Driven by this overwhelming paralysis, I found myself turning away from the glowing screens and walking out into a neglected, weed-choked corner of my yard. I needed to touch something real, something that did not operate on algorithms or outrage. Armed with a simple iron spade, a bag of compost, and a few packets of seeds, I decided to mark out a modest four-by-eight-foot garden plot. 

The work was immediately, punishingly physical. I plunged the blade into the sun-baked earth, turning over compacted clay, wrestling with stubborn taproots, and hauling heavy stones out of the dirt. Sweat stung my eyes, my lower back throbbed, and soil caked beneath my fingernails. Yet, within hours of this manual labor, a strange quiet descended upon my mind. The abstract, suffocating anxieties that had occupied my thoughts were driven out by the immediate, tactile reality of the soil. My world, which had felt terrifyingly vast and uncontrollable, narrowed to the precise dimensions of the earth beneath my knees.

As the weeks passed, the garden transformed from a patch of dirt into an intimate sanctuary. I learned the distinct texture of healthy soil, rich with dark organic matter and teeming with earthworms. I watched with quiet awe as microscopic seeds, watered and tended, split open to push fragile green tendrils up through the darkness. In this microscopic world, time moved at a different pace—neither rushed by the panic of the news cycle nor halted by despair, but governed by the ancient, steady rhythms of sun, rain, and decay. 

Kneeling in the dirt, I began to experience a profound sense of grounding. The garden did not offer an escape from reality, but rather a deeper immersion into it. It reminded me that despite human folly and destructive violence, the earth retains an extraordinary, quiet capacity for renewal. To plant a seed is an act of defiance; it is a declaration of belief in tomorrow.

Cultivating this small plot of land has not stopped the melting of ice caps, nor has it halted distant wars. But it has altered something fundamental within me. It has taught me that small, intimate rituals are not futile simply because they cannot fix the world. Instead, they are the very things that sustain us within it. By anchoring ourselves to the tangible, living earth, we gather the spiritual nourishment and resilience required to face the storm—reminding us that even in an era of overwhelming chaos, life remains a gift worth tending.
outputs.L5:
For thirty years, Will’s life was defined by the rugged coastlines and crisp, snow-dusted autumns of Massachusetts. Raised in a historic town just outside of Boston, he was accustomed to the fast-paced, stoic energy of New England. His roots were buried deep in the Bay State's stony soil, and he fully expected to spend the rest of his days there.

Everything changed the afternoon a family lawyer read his late grandfather’s last will and testament. To Will’s complete astonishment, he had been left a sprawling, slightly overgrown peach orchard tucked away in the countryside of Georgia. 

Driven by a sudden need for change, Will decided to take the leap. He packed his life into a pickup truck, leaving the chilly winds and brick-lined streets of Massachusetts behind for the sweet, humid air of the American South. 

The transition was a shock to his system. Georgia was a world of red clay, draped Spanish moss, and slow, sun-drenched afternoons on front porches. The quiet hospitality stood in stark contrast to the sharp, efficient rhythm of his hometown.

At first, the unfamiliar climate and demanding work of running the orchard tested his resolve. But as the seasons turned, Will found a surprising harmony between his two lives. The resilience he had forged during harsh Massachusetts winters gave him the determination to restore the farm, while the warmth of Georgia taught him to slow down and appreciate the present moment. 

It was an unexpected journey—one set in motion by a legal will, carried out by a man named Will, and rooted in the iron strength of his own personal will to build a new home in Southern soil.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a five-part prose poem contrasting global climate anxiety and world news with the quiet, personal act of gardening. Number each section 1 to 5. In section 1, mention a radio report about shifting climate zones (e.g., Massachusetts feeling like Georgia by 2050). In section 4, reference a film on gleaning and a quote about spiritual hunger.
counterfactuals.output:
**1.**  
The radio sitting on the potting bench crackles through a haze of static and distant lightning. A broadcaster’s steady, uninflected voice reports on the relentless northward migration of hardiness zones, explaining that by 2050, the damp, cool woods of Massachusetts will carry the sweltering, subtropical breath of Georgia. My hands are plunged up to the wrists in April mud that still holds the phantom chill of an old-world winter. The news speaks of a planet in quiet, terrifying transit, redrawing its maps while we sleep. Beneath my fingernails, the soil is dark and indifferent; I hold a tender heirloom tomato seedling in my palm, wondering what language its roots will have to learn when the air finally turns to fire.

**2.**  
In my pocket, the phone vibrates with the rhythm of global catastrophe: wild blazes consuming ancient forests, rivers shrinking into cracked clay, refugees walking along scorched highways. I press the screen face-down into the clover. Here, in the micro-realm of the raised beds, the news arrives at the speed of sap. The headlines are written in the silvery trails of slugs, the white powder of mildew on a cucumber leaf, the silent siege of bindweed crawling up the trellis. It feels almost absurd—an act of frivolous, selfish privilege—to spend an afternoon delicately pruning suckers from a vine while the world burns in real time. Yet the dirt demands a hyper-local fidelity; it asks only for the small, quiet attention of a hand wielding a trowel.

**3.**  
Climate dread is a light-speed phenomenon, arriving in instant, terrifying bursts through glass screens. But the garden operates in a slow, stubborn counter-time. It takes three seasons for an oak leaf to soften into black humus, four months for a garlic clove to split into a silver crown beneath the snow. In the silence between push notifications, I watch the earthworms turn panic into fertility. To dig is to step out of the frantic, apocalyptic march of human history and enter a circle. Here, decomposition is not the end of the world, but merely the heavy, damp blanket under which tomorrow’s green shoot is secretly constructed. 

**4.**  
I am reminded of Agnès Varda’s film on the art of gleaning, where the camera follows those who stoop in harvested fields to collect what the heavy machinery leaves behind—knotted potatoes, missed grapes, the discarded heart-shaped remnants of a crop. The film echoes a timeless truth about our modern condition: *“There is a spiritual hunger in us that no market can satisfy, a longing to gather the forgotten fragments of the earth.”* We have become gleaners of a fragile era, wandering the edges of a changing climate, searching for scraps of beauty amidst ecological loss. As I bend low to pick a handful of wind-fallen, bruised plums from the grass, I feel that quiet, aching hunger—not for sustenance, but for a sacred reconciliation with a world we are so rapidly undoing.

**5.**  
Dusk settles over the yard like cool, grey ash. The radio has sputtered out, and the phone screen remains dark. In the gathering shadow, I push winter bulbs deep into the cool earth, planting life for a season that will inevitably be warmer, stranger, and more uncertain than the one fading around me tonight. This garden will not reverse the thermal shifts, nor will it cool the warming seas. It is simply a quiet testament, a stubborn posture of care in an age of ruin. I turn the brass tap, wash the dark loam from my knuckles, and watch the muddy water sink into the thirsty soil—carrying the dust of today down to feed the roots of an unpredictable tomorrow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a reflective, slightly fragmented piece divided into 5 numbered parts? It should contrast terrifying global realities like war, oil spills, and climate collapse with the small, daydream-like act of planting a backyard plot of cucumbers and zucchini.
counterfactuals.output:
**1.**

There is grit under my fingernails. Cold, dark compost, rich with the rot of last winter’s leaves. 

In my back pocket, the phone vibrates again. A muted, persistent humming against my hip. The screen lights up the dark fabric of my denim: *Breaking.* A missile strike on a grid. A plume of obsidian smoke over the Black Sea. A tanker cracking open like a hollow tooth, leaking three million gallons of heavy crude into the nursery grounds of blue whales. 

I turn the phone face down in the grass. 

I push my thumb into the earth. One inch. Two inches. The soil resists, then yields. It smells of earthworms and ancient rain. I drop a single cucumber seed into the dark. It is small, pale, and dry, no larger than a tear. I push the dirt back over it and pat it flat, as if tucking a child into bed while the house burns down around us.

**2.**

The geometry of the world is jagged now. 

Shattered concrete in suburban neighborhoods six thousand miles away. Steel rebar blooming like iron weeds from blasted brick. On satellite imagery, the oil slicks look like iridescent oil-cloth spread across a blue table—thin, beautiful, suffocating. The ocean holds its breath. The coral bleeds white in water that has grown as warm as bathwater. 

Everything is too hot. Everything is leaking, or burning, or being shelled into dust. 

And here: a four-by-eight wooden frame. Cedar boards I bought at the hardware store from a teenager who looked too tired to be seventeen. Inside the frame, two packets of seed. *Cucurbita pepo.* *Cucumis sativus.* 

It feels like an absurdity. A hallucination. A childish play-act at survival. The globe is melting at the poles, and I am standing in a patch of dandelions with a green plastic watering can, playing God to three square feet of mud.

**3.**

A zucchini seed looks like a sliver of dried wood. Flat. Papery. Completely devoid of grace. 

To press it into the dirt requires a violent act of faith—or perhaps just a profound, deliberate numbness. It demands that you believe in a *sixty days from now*. It demands you assume the sky will not turn the color of ash before July. That the tap will still yield water when turned. That the supply chains, the weather patterns, the fragile treaties holding back the hungry machines will hold for just eight more weeks. 

Just long enough for yellow blossoms to open. 

Is it hope? Or is it a psychological defensive maneuver? A way to shrink the catastrophe down until it fits inside a garden plot, where the only enemy is a striped cucumber beetle or a sudden late frost.

**4.**

The sky today is an uncanny, bruised peach. 

The wind carries smoke from fires three states away—pines that stood for two centuries, reduced to orange static in an afternoon. My eyes sting. The sunlight hits the lawn at an unnatural angle, diffused through a haze of particulate matter and carbon. 

I fill the watering can. The water comes from a reservoir that is currently at twenty-four percent capacity. Every drop I pour onto these seedbeds is a stolen luxury, a tiny act of treason against the coming drought. 

I watch the dry dirt drink. It sizzles faintly. 

Somewhere, a drone hovers over a muddy trench, searching for heat signatures. Somewhere, a pelican tries to scrape slick, heavy black sludge from its chest feathers with a beak that wasn't built for industrial waste. 

I pour another splash over the spot where the zucchini is supposed to rise. The water settles, reflecting a sun that looks like a dim red coin through the haze.

**5.**

Two weeks pass. The headlines do not soften. 

The heat dome expands. The casualty counts tick upward in neat, sans-serif fonts on glass screens. The ice shelves crack with the sound of thunder that no human ear is near enough to hear.

And then, this morning: a crack in the dirt. 

A pale, looped stem pushes through the soil, dragging its seed coat with it like an old coat. By noon, it uncurls. Two thick, oval leaves—bright, impossibly green, covered in fine silver hair. Beside it, another. The cucumbers are coming up in a straight, orderly line.

They do not know about the oil in the sea. They do not know about the artillery shells or the methane bubbling from the melting tundra. They only know the light, dim as it is, and the moisture in the dark earth.

They want to grow. They want to spread their prickly vines across the dust, to bloom into loud, yellow star-flowers, to bear heavy, cool fruit that is ninety-six percent water.

I sit on my heels in the grass. The air smells of ozone and distant burning pine. I touch the small green leaf with the tip of my finger. It is soft. It is cold. It is completely defenceless. 

We live at the end of something. We lie down in the wreckage every night. But this morning, the earth gave up a leaf, and I am foolish enough to be grateful.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a 5-part eco-poetry text that touches on spiritual hunger versus physical hunger, referencing Agnès Varda's documentary on gleaners, shifting agricultural zones, and the feeling of connection to the earth while digging in the dirt.
counterfactuals.output:
**I. Humus (The First Dig)**

Press the thumbs into cold, unspooled clay—  
here, beneath the lawn’s bright, plastic green,  
lies the slow dark, the old memory.  
To sink ten fingers into damp silt  
is to plug a severed cable back into the wall of the world.  
The earth beneath the fingernails forms dark half-moons,  
grief-stains of loam, petrichor rising like incense.  
In the press of rot and wriggling earthworms,  
the skin forgets its solitary skin.  
My palm becomes a taproot;  
the soil holds my pulse  
and does not ask what I have earned today,  
only that I stay down long enough  
to remember what I am made of.

***

**II. *Les Glaneuses* (The Leftover Field)**

We stand in the furrows after the tractors depart,  
shadows bent like scythes against the stubble.  
Agnès held her small digital lens to the highway,  
framing trucks that carried away the symmetrical, the perfect,  
and walked the mud for the forgotten:  
the misshapen, the oversized,  
the heart-shaped potato tossed into the ditch  
because no machine could measure its love.  
To glean is to bend the spine to what remains.  
Physical hunger searches the dirt for calories,  
for the overlooked turnip, the bruised apple.  
It is an honest, desperate stooping.  
The camera pans over the old woman's wrinkled hands—  
she gathers not just food, but time,  
rescuing the rejected flesh of the field  
from the cold mouth of oblivion.

***

**III. The Two Maws**

The stomach is an easy beast to tame:  
a bowl of steamed grain, a handful of salt,  
a wild onion tugged from the ditch will quiet its barking.  
It asks only for mass, for fuel to turn the wheel.  
But the second maw—  
the hollow beneath the ribs—  
is a cavern that swallows whole cities and remains empty.  
We live in an age of bloated bellies and starved ghosts,  
surfeited on ultra-processed sunlight,  
wrapped in sterile plastic, far from the rot.  
We swallow thousands of calories a day  
and still faint from a profound, terrifying malnutrition.  
The body is full, but the spirit prowls the aisles,  
licking the glass of a world it can no longer touch,  
famished for the bitter taste of wildness,  
dying for a handful of real dirt.

***

**IV. The Shifting Meridians**

The maps are melting at the edges.  
The hardiness zones creep north like fleeing animals;  
the corn belt abandons its ancestral floor,  
drifting toward the boreal shield.  
In the south, the olive trees bake in their own ancient oil,  
their blossoms scorched before the fruit can set.  
The peach orchards forget the frost they need to dream.  
Farmers hold soil that no longer speaks their grandfather’s language,  
watching the rain arrive in violent torrents  
or not at all.  
The geography of our bread is migrating.  
We are left chasing the temperate fringe,  
gleaners not just of leftover crops,  
but of shifting climates,  
trying to plant tomorrow's seeds in a soil  
that changes its name with every season.

***

**V. The Sacred Meal**

So I kneel again in the unstable dirt.  
If the zone moves, let my knees move with it.  
I dig until my hands are cold,  
until the scent of fungal networks and wet decay  
fills the void behind my sternum.  
Here, where physical hunger meets its humble root,  
the spiritual famine begins to ease.  
The earth offers no grand, immortal theology—  
only the quiet grace of rot turning into clover,  
only the heart-shaped tuber found in the mud,  
imperfect, heavy, and real.  
I do not need to possess the field;  
I only need to yield to its slow, turning wheel.  
I take the dirt into my palms,  
and for a moment,  
the beast inside me stops prowling,  
looks down at its muddy hands,  
and is fed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a 5-section prose poem about gardening as an emotional and spiritual response to global climate collapse.
counterfactuals.output:
**I. The Shift from the Screen**

The sky has become a haunted kiln, heavy with the ash of burning boreal forests and the static of broken seasons. We live in the paralyzing geometry of the scroll, where whole ecosystems vanish between tap and swipe, leaving our chests filled with an unexhaled, global grief. To step outside is to cross a threshold from the abstract horror of numbers into the immediate mercy of the physical world. I drop to my knees on the scorched perimeter of the lawn, letting my forehead touch the dry grass. The atmosphere above is unravelling, but the soil beneath my palms is still cold, dense, and real. Here, the frantic rhythm of human panic slows to match the patient pulse of deep time.


**II. The Sacrament of Dirt**

To dig is to enter a confessional where no words are requested. I sink the spade into the compacted earth, breaking through the crust of a land we have overworked and misunderstood. My fingers churn through dust, silt, and the ancient detritus of decayed leaves—a vast graveyard that doubles as a womb. In an age of synthetic noise and melting ice, dirt remains the only entirely honest thing left; it remembers every drought and holds space for every future root. I bury my hands in the dark dampness, feeling the blind, steady travel of an earthworm. It is a secular baptism, washing away the paralysis of the end-times with the unvarnished weight of the ground.


**III. Audacious Liturgies**

There is a wild, holy foolishness in holding a wrinkled tomato seed while the news predicts another season of record-breaking heat. Each tiny, dormant speck is a sealed prophecy, a quiet wager against the void. I press them into small, dark furrows, pouring water from a dented can, whispering an ancient agreement into the soil: *I will tend you, if you will endure.* Planting anything now is not an act of ignorance; it is an act of radical defiance. We know the summer may scorch the vines or drown the roots, yet we measure out our remaining days in the green, stubborn geometry of shoots breaking through the crust.


**IV. The Ark of Soft Alliances**

Over time, the garden transforms into a sanctuary floating on an ocean of ecological uncertainty. I learn to speak a dialect older than despair—the quiet transactions between nitrogen-fixing clover and exhausted soil, the frantic, dusted music of a solitary bee inside a squash blossom. When macro-systems fail, this small patch of land becomes a place of fierce interspecies solidarity. I leave shallow dishes of water for birds disoriented by the shifting winds; the marigolds lend their sharp fragrance to protect the soft leaves of brassicas. We are all refugees of the same altered climate, huddled together in this small sanctuary, teaching one another how to survive the storm.


**V. Grace in the Ruins**

This small plot will not refreeze the melting poles, nor will it turn back the rising tides. It is a fragile altar built in the twilight of an era. Yet, as I harvest sun-warmed basil and bruised figs, I understand that spiritual survival was never about escaping the end; it was about how deeply we could love the world while it was here. Gardening at the end of nature is a prayer of radically limited scale—a stubborn, quiet devotion to the present tense. If the world must break, let it find us with dark earth under our fingernails, tending to a flower that insists on blooming anyway, right here, on the edge of the ruin.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
